extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of mathematical problem solving (high-school / undergraduate) and general problem-solvers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical heuristics and standards for analyzing, modeling, and solving mathematical and engineering problems: how to identify unknowns/data/conditions, mobilize and organize knowledge, vary problems, use approximations, and apply proof techniques (direct, indirect, reductio).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish unknowns, data, and conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal parts of a 'problem to find' are the unknown, the data, and the condition; for a 'problem to prove' the principal parts are the hypothesis and the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly ask: What is the unknown? What are the data? What is the condition? (For proofs: What is the hypothesis? What is the conclusion?) Separate the various parts of the condition/hypothesis and find the connection between data and unknown or between hypothesis and conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify and define concepts used
rubrics_metrics.description: In practical problems concepts and necessary preliminary knowledge are often 'more complex and less sharply defined' than in mathematical problems; clarification of concepts may become an important part of the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check 'Have you taken into account all essential notions involved in the problem?' and, where notions are hazy, work to make them precise before proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobilization of relevant prior knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Solving a problem requires recollecting and selecting relevant items of previously acquired knowledge (formerly solved problems, known theorems, definitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: Have you seen this before? Do you know a related problem? Do you know a theorem that could be useful? Mobilize those elements from memory as raw material for the solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization (adapt and combine recalled material)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recollected facts must be combined into an argument well adapted to the problem at hand; mobilization and organization are two aspects of the same process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct an argument that connects the mobilized materials into a coherent whole; look for how to adapt known methods or results to fit the present problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation of the problem (restate, generalize, specialize)
rubrics_metrics.description: Progress often requires changing the problem: restating it, using analogy, generalization, specialization, decomposing and recombining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try: Could you restate the problem? Could you restate it differently? Could you keep only part of the condition and drop others? Use DEFINITION, ANALOGY, GENERALIZATION, SPECIALIZATION, DECOMPOSING and RECOMBINING as concrete variation methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the heuristic checklist of questions
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of specific questions and suggestions aimed at mobilization, organization, variation, and forecasting the solution steps is applicable to all kinds of problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative questions: What is the unknown/data/condition? Separate parts of the condition. Find the connection between data and unknown. Look at the unknown and think of familiar similar problems. Keep only part of the condition — how does the unknown vary? Could you derive something useful from the data? Could you change the unknown or the data so they are nearer? Did you use all the data? Did you use the whole condition? For proofs: separate hypothesis and conclusion; is the conclusion still valid if part of the hypothesis is dropped? Could you think of another hypothesis that yields the conclusion?

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide which data/conditions to neglect (practical problems)
rubrics_metrics.description: In practical problems the data and conditions are often inexhaustible; one must decide which items appreciably influence the solution and neglect the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modify questions like 'Did you use all the data?' to 'Did you use all the data which could contribute appreciably to the solution?' Collect relevant information but 'draw the line somewhere' and accept that some uncertainty remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximations and model simplification
rubrics_metrics.description: When deriving mathematical problems from practical problems, it is reasonable to neglect minor data and allow slight inaccuracy to gain simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose approximations that yield practical simplicity without losing significant accuracy (example: assume the Earth is a sphere for many map problems). Balance simplicity vs accuracy consciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress indicators: mobilization, organization, conception change, prevision
rubrics_metrics.description: Progress toward a solution consists in advancing mobilization/organization of knowledge, evolving the conception of the problem, and increasing foresight (prevision) of the steps to the final argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge progress by whether more relevant material has been recalled and organized, whether the problem conception is fuller, and whether you can foresee steps leading to the solution; expect both steady small advances and occasional abrupt 'bright ideas.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage heuristic (plausible) reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Before obtaining certainty, we often must be satisfied with plausible, provisional considerations to guide discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conjectures, plausible guesses, and provisional plans to explore promising directions — these are essential for discovery even though they are not final proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek and provoke 'bright ideas' (insight moments)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'bright idea' or 'brain-wave' is an abrupt, momentous reorganization of outlook leading to sudden progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare for such insights by understanding the problem deeply, varying viewpoints, and provoking the idea through the heuristic questions and trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decompose large problems and solve auxiliary/partial problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Large or complex problems often have distinct parts; solve related smaller problems or construct partial solutions to approach the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try solving related problems using some of the letters/conditions (puzzle example), form progressively longer/closer approximations, and identify standard endings or components (e.g., common suffixes) to reduce the search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply analogy and reuse known solutions/methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for familiar problems with the same or similar unknown/conclusion and consider using their results or methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: Could you use a previously solved related problem? Could you use its result or method? Should you introduce an auxiliary element to make its use possible?

rubrics_metrics.name: Test sufficiency, redundancy, and contradiction of conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate whether the condition/data are sufficient, insufficient, redundant, or contradictory for determining the unknown or proving the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try dropping parts of the condition, keeping only part, or altering hypothesis/conclusion to see what remains provable or derivable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reductio ad absurdum to show impossibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Reductio ad absurdum shows the falsity of an assumption by deriving from it a manifest absurdity; useful to prove impossibility or incompatibility of parts of the condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: Suppose hypothetically that the full condition is satisfied; translate that situation into equations/expressions; find a contradiction (a non-integer count, an impossibility such as divisibility contradiction); conclude the original supposition is false. Example: showing it's impossible to write numbers using each digit once with sum 100 by deriving a non-integer t or divisibility contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use indirect proof (disprove the opposite) and combine with reductio
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect proof establishes truth by showing the falsity of the opposite assumption; often combined with reductio ad absurdum (e.g., Euclid's proof of infinitely many primes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Face the unlikely contrary situation, derive a manifest absurdity (e.g., construct Q=(product of known primes)+1) and conclude the original claim is true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of objections to indirect/reductio methods (exposition vs discovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect proofs and long reductio sequences can be pedagogically awkward because they require holding a false assumption in mind; they may be harder to retain for learners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish use as a research/discovery tool (valuable) from use as exposition (may be painful); where possible convert or rearrange indirect proofs into direct or more pleasant forms for presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert reductio/indirect arguments into positive/direct assertions when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: After using reductio or indirect proof to discover a result, attempt to extract independent true parts or restate the problem so that the argument becomes constructive or direct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: From reductio that sum = 10t+(45−t) is divisible by 9, present the direct divisibility argument and drop the long hypotheticals; convert 'there is no last prime' into 'given primes 2..P, find a new prime' (constructive reformulation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stop data collection when further data are unlikely to change solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Because practical problems can offer inexhaustible data, one must decide when additional information is unnecessary for an appreciable change in solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh costs and benefits of more data; accept a margin of uncertainty and proceed once you have enough information that appreciably affects the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: When stuck, try multiple restatements and viewpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Working from different standpoints and viewing the problem from different sides enriches conception and often reveals workable approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically attempt restatements, diagrams ('Draw a figure'), separate components (vowels/consonants in anagram), or other reorganizations to stimulate new trials.
